title: The School of Rock
full_review:
An unemployed rocker desperate for cash takes a job posing as a substitute teacher at a tony prep school in director Richard Linklater's lukewarm laugher "School of Rock" (Paramount).

Despite some humorous riffs, the film's upbeat and amped-up message about pursuing one's dreams -- think Jimi Hendrix meets "Dead Poets Society" -- is undermined by a problematic bass rhythm that pokes fun at parental authority and the value of any subject that can't be learned on an electric guitar.

Providing lead vocals is Jack Black, who plays Dewey Finn, a rock 'n' roll prophet who finds himself voted out by band mates weeks before they are to perform at a local battle-of-the-bands competition. Dewey's best friend and roommate, Ned (Mike White), a spineless substitute teacher, doesn't have the heart to demand back-rent from his freeloading buddy. Ned's lack of backbone is a constant cause of friction between him and his live-in girlfriend, Patty (Sarah Silverman), an opinionated harpy who, unlike Ned, excels at kicking slackers while they're down.

Dewey's dead-end situation takes an unexpected turn when he picks up a phone call intended for Ned and impulsively accepts a gig at a prestigious elementary school from its uptight, by-the-book principal, Rosalie Mullins (Joan Cusack) -- who thinks she has just hired his highly qualified roommate.

Dewey quickly finds out that supervising a room full of fourth graders is a lot tougher than playing a riff of Deep Purple's "Smoke on the Water" with mittens on. Nevertheless, he manages to sleep through most of the school day, to the dismay of the class' precocious smarty-pants, Summer (Miranda Cosgrove), who thinks Dewey's self-imposed all-day recess is a waste of tuition money.

Dewey's slacker syllabus changes when he overhears the children performing during music class. With his eyes still set on the upcoming battle of the bands, Dewey sets about molding them into a rock band, telling them it is for a school project. Evading the ever-watchful eyes of Principal Mullins, Dewey introduces rock 'n' roll into the academy's reading, 'riting and 'rithmetic curriculum. Predictably, he instills his students with a newfound passion and gets several of them to emerge from their emotional shells along the way.

While the film imparts a positive message about pursuing one's dreams, it does so in a tone that mocks traditional authority figures such as parents and teachers, which is made more palatable to young viewers by Black's impressive, high-voltage performance. Throughout the movie, Dewey refers to authority figures as "the man," whose oppressive yoke must be thrown off by the liberating power of high-decibel music.

Equally troubling to parents is the movie's cavalier and highly irresponsible (even if unintended) suggestion that, once students have been thus enlightened by rock 'n' roll, they need not be bothered by such trivial subjects as math and literature. In fact, during one scene Dewey tells one of his wards to put down the book he is reading in order to rehearse the song they will perform at the competition -- hardly a cause for laughter given the current state of American education.

And while its celebration of rock 'n' roll music is not in itself a bad thing, the film offers a rather one-sided picture of rock culture, extolling the passion and creativity of its proponents, while sugar-coating its darker side. At one point Dewey pulls one of his students out of a van of pot-smoking musicians, counseling him that "true rock" is not about getting high but about the "music." This lame public-service-announcement moment seems disingenuous if not outright dishonest, since the movie gives no mention to the many rock icons -- many of whose musical merits are extolled by Dewey -- who destroyed their lives through drugs.

In addition to some crude beer humor, the film also introduces a running gag concerning an effete male student, which, while refraining from any sexual innuendo, is altogether unnecessary. Beyond some forced laughs elicited by the fey fourth-grader's "Queer-Eye-for-the-Grade-School-Guy" style sense, the joke seems out of place, serving no narrative purpose beyond acculturating an acceptance of the gay lifestyle at even the grammar school level.

In the school of tough grading, "School of Rock" should receive just a passing mark.

Due to some crude humor and language, as well as several drug references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
